Abstract Peer report of aggression has typically been obtained through peer nominations. The purpose of this study was to identify the extent to which peer nominations and peer ratings identified the same children as aggressive and to explore whether the two methods were equally accurate in identifying children at risk for poor social adjustment. Participants were 1051 students in third, fourth, or fifth grade and were predominantly African American (76.6%). Participants provided self-report of sympathy and peer nominations and ratings of overt and relational aggression, prosocial behavior, and leadership. Teachers reported on participants’ school adjustment. Peer nominations and peer ratings of aggressive behavior were closely related. Peer ratings of overt and relational aggression emerged as a unique predictor of all indicators of adjustment, whereas peer nominations were uniquely associated with three of six outcomes of interest. Peer ratings are a promising approach to assessing aggression and may address problems of consumer acceptance. Keywords: aggression, peer report, measurement, children, adjustment ---------------------------------------- Aggression during childhood and adolescence is common. However, when it occurs frequently, it can have a significant negative impact on children’s short- and long-term psychosocial and academic adjustment (e.g., Card, Stucky, Sawalani, & Little, 2008). One ongoing discussion in the study of youth aggression is how best to measure it. Measurement of aggression is used for many purposes, such as collecting prevalence data, identifying high-risk children, and understanding risk and protective factors as well as outcomes associated with aggressive behavior (Branson & Cornell, 2009; Farrell, Sullivan, Goncy, & Le, 2015). When selecting instruments, researchers need reliable and valid measures of aggression that balance potentially competing goals of accuracy, thoroughness, cost-effectiveness, acceptability, and logistic ease. The purpose of this study is to compare two methods of peer report of children’s aggressive behavior—peer nominations and peer ratings—in order to explore the extent to which the different methods identify the same children as overtly or relationally aggressive, and to examine the patterns of relations between peer nominations and peer ratings of aggression and children’s social adjustment. Given that peer nominations have been somewhat controversial (e.g., Orpinas & Horne), it is important to examine whether there are effective, alternative methods to measure children’s aggression, such as peer ratings. Peer-targeted aggression may take different forms. Overt aggression includes physical aggression (e.g., pushing, hitting, kicking) and verbal aggression (e.g., mocking, name-calling; Martin & Huebner, 2007). Relational aggression, which targets an individual’s social relationships, status, and reputation, is a form of aggression that can involve rumor spreading and deliberately excluding or socially isolating another person (Crick & Grotpeter, 1995). There is a significant, moderate correlation between overt and relational aggression (Sullivan, Farrell, & Kliewer, 2006; Underwood, Beron, & Rosen, 2010), but prior research has shown that there may be differences in how each form of aggression relates to children’s psychosocial adjustment, including academic achievement, delinquency, social adjustment, and depressive symptoms (e.g., Preddy & Fite, 2012; Putallaz et al., 2007; van der Wal, de Wit, & Hirasing, 2003). These findings provide support for measuring overt and relational aggression separately, and thus, for separately exploring the best way to measure each form of aggression in this study. Although some studies use direct observation or archival data such as discipline referrals to measure youth aggression, the most common approach is to use survey methods (c.f. Wilson, Lipsey, & Derzon, 2003). Direct observational methods are not ideal to assess children’s low-frequency behaviors, especially behaviors in which they are less likely to engage in the presence of adults, such as aggression; direct observations are also time-intensive and costly (Orpinas & Horne, 2006). Related to archival data, schools vary in their thresholds for making discipline referrals, their documentation practices, and the consistency of their treatment across children, making it difficult to draw conclusions across teachers and schools (Farrell et al., 2015; Orpinas & Horne, 2006). Currently, the most popular approach to measure a child’s aggressive behavior is via surveys, through informants such as child self-report, parents, teachers, and peers. There are benefits and drawbacks to assessing aggression through each type of informant (e.g., Farrell et al., 2015; Orpinas & Horne, 2006). Given that peers observe their classmates in multiple contexts, including locations where there is less adult supervision (e.g., playground, lunchroom, hallways; Leff, Costigan, & Power, 2004), they may be able to provide a more holistic report of children’s aggression. Additionally, peer-report measures by definition include multiple informants, so that the resultant scores are not based on one person’s opinion, in contrast to parent-, teacher-, or self-report measures (Bukowski, Cillessen, & Velásquez, 2012). fetched_contents.text: Full article: Concurrent Validity of the Olweus Bully/Victim Questionnaire Abstract This study examined the concurrent validity of the Olweus Bully/Victim Questionnaire (BVQ) in a convenience sample of 202 middle school students in central Virginia. This appears to be the first published study to compare BVQ reports of being bullied and of bullying others with independent criteria not subject to shared method variance. Self-reported bullying on the BVQ was significantly correlated with peer nominations for bullying (r = .12, p < .05) and academic grades (r = −.15, p < .05), but not disciplinary infractions. Self-reported victimization was significantly correlated with peer nominations for victimization (r = .42, p < .01) and academic grades (r = −.12, p < .01). These results provide only modest support for the concurrent validity of the BVQ and raise concern about reliance on student self-report to measure school bullying. Self-report surveys are the most frequently used measures to evaluate the success of anti-bullying programs and estimate the prevalence of bullying in schools (CitationCornell, Sheras, & Cole, 2006). Self-report measures are a rapid and efficient method of gathering data from large numbers of students; however, there is limited research available on their reliability and validity (CitationCornell et al., 2006; CitationGriffin & Gross, 2004; CitationLeff, Power, & Goldstein, 2004). Self-report bullying surveys are usually measured on an anonymous basis, so that researchers are unable to corroborate student reports or assess their relationship to any independent criteria. This measurement strategy has a profound effect on the field, because the vast majority of bullying research and bullying prevention efforts rely on anonymous self-report measures of unproven validity (CitationCornell et al., 2006). The conventional wisdom is that it is necessary to use an anonymous survey in order for students to be willing to provide honest answers; however, there is reason to question this assumption. Three studies have compared anonymous and nonanonymous versions of the same survey to determine whether students are less likely to admit bullying or other problem behaviors when their identity is not anonymous. In a sample of 704 Dutch adolescents, approximately half of the students received questionnaires labeled with their names, but were assured of confidentiality, while the other half were told that their responses would not be connected to their identity in any way (CitationVan de Looij-Jansen, Goldschmeding, & Jan de Wilde, 2006). They found no significant differences between the two groups in reporting bullying, as well as carrying a weapon, using hard drugs, or being truant from school. Another study by CitationChan, Myron, and Crawshaw (2005) investigated differences between anonymous versus confidential self-reports of bullying and victimization on the School Life Survey (SLS; CitationChan, 2002), a self-report questionnaire designed to measure bullying. The SLS was administered to 562 students (ages 6–13) from 30 classrooms. Students were randomly assigned to write their full names on the survey or to take the survey anonymously. There were no significant group differences in reported rates of bullying behaviors or victimization experiences such as hitting, teasing, and lying about other students. CitationO'Malley, Johnston, Bachman, and Schulenberg (2000) examined the difference between anonymous and confidential reporting on the Monitoring The Future Survey, which is administered annually to nationally representative samples of adolescents in the United States. The survey has a lengthy series of questions concerning personal use of illegal drugs and alcohol, as well as delinquent behaviors such as stealing and weapon-carrying. In this study of more than 34,000 students, half of the youths were administered the survey with explicit assurance that their answers were anonymous and so could not be linked to them, while the other half were told that their answers would be held in confidence, but were required to report their name and address to the researchers. There was little or no difference in the reporting of sensitive information under the two conditions (CitationO'Malley et al., 2000). Branch report: methodological strengths and weaknesses of peer nomination

Peer nomination is a widely used method for measuring bullying because it leverages multiple informants rather than relying on a single individual’s self-assessment [N1-F1]. In practice, peer nominations involve asking students to identify classmates who bully others or are bullied, and the resulting data can capture bullying that may be underreported by victims because victims are not the only source of information [N2-F2]. This is a major strength: peer nominations can detect bullying that victims may not disclose, especially if victims are reluctant to report due to fear, shame, or social consequences [N2-F2]. The same evidence also notes that peer nominations are often used to measure aggression in school settings where direct observation is impractical, because peer informants can observe behavior in settings with less adult supervision such as playgrounds and hallways [N1-F1].

A key limitation of peer nomination is that it can be biased by social desirability and group dynamics. The literature described in the peer-report literature indicates that peer nominations are not immune to problems of consumer acceptance and that the resulting scores depend on the composition of the informant group [N1-F1]. In the concurrent validity study of the Olweus Bully/Victim Questionnaire, self-reported bullying was only modestly correlated with peer nominations, suggesting that peer nominations may not fully capture the same construct in the same way [N2-F2]. This implies that peer nominations can be influenced by social pressures, such as the tendency of students to nominate someone as a bully or victim in ways that conform to group norms or to avoid conflict [N2-F2]. The same source also emphasizes that peer-report measures are often based on multiple informants, but this does not eliminate measurement issues [N1-F1].

Reliability and validity of peer nomination depend on sample size, grade level, and informant selection. The peer-report literature cited here reports that peer nominations and peer ratings were closely related, but peer ratings were uniquely associated with adjustment outcomes in a sample of third, fourth, and fifth graders [N1-F1]. This suggests that younger students may have different reporting patterns and that grade level can affect the accuracy of the measure. The classroom-size study further shows that classroom size was negatively associated with peer-reported bullying and victimization in both samples, and with self-reported bullying and victimization in the Dutch sample only [N4-F3]. This indicates that informant selection and classroom context matter: smaller classrooms may change how peers perceive and report bullying, and the same measure can yield different results depending on whether peers are in a classroom of a certain size [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that peer nominations can be affected by how bullying is defined and operationalized, because prevalence estimates can vary across studies [N2-R2].

Overall, peer nomination is strongest when the goal is to detect bullying that victims may not report and when multiple informants are available to reduce reliance on a single perspective [N1-F1]. Its weaknesses include social desirability bias, group dynamics, and dependence on informant composition and classroom context [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

Branch report: methodological strengths and weaknesses of self-report methods

Self-report methods are attractive because they can capture private or less obvious bullying experiences that may not be observed by peers or teachers. The evidence provided here states that self-report measures are the most frequently used way to evaluate anti-bullying programs and estimate bullying prevalence, and that they are rapid and efficient for gathering data from large numbers of students [N2-F2]. This efficiency is a major strength, especially when researchers want broad coverage and quick data collection. The same source also notes that self-report surveys are usually anonymous, which is often assumed to increase honesty, although the evidence cited here questions whether anonymity is always necessary [N2-F2]. Because self-reports can include experiences that are difficult to observe directly, they are useful for capturing bullying that occurs in private, less visible, or less socially sanctioned forms [N2-F2].

A major weakness of self-report methods is social desirability bias and other response biases. The Olweus Bully/Victim Questionnaire study found modest concurrent validity for self-reported bullying and victimization, and it emphasized that self-report surveys are often anonymous, so researchers cannot corroborate student reports or assess them against independent criteria [N2-F2]. This lack of corroboration makes self-report methods vulnerable to socially desirable responses, where students may underreport bullying because they fear judgment, or overreport in ways that fit a socially acceptable narrative [N2-F2]. The evidence also highlights recall bias and response style effects: anonymous versus nonanonymous survey conditions did not produce meaningful differences in bullying reporting in some studies, but this does not eliminate the broader risk that students’ memories or response styles can distort prevalence estimates [N2-F2]. In addition, the search evidence notes that wording choices, such as whether the survey asks about “bully” or “bullying,” can affect responses [N2-R5], indicating that self-report methods are sensitive to how bullying is operationalized.

Reliability and validity of self-report methods depend on question wording, anonymity, and respondent age. The evidence explicitly links wording to prevalence estimates, stating that the choice of the word “bully” in survey items can influence reported bullying behavior [N2-R5]. This supports the conclusion that wording matters: clearer, more youth-friendly definitions may improve validity, while ambiguous wording can produce inconsistent results [N2-R5]. Anonymity is also important because anonymous surveys are common, but the same evidence suggests that anonymity alone does not guarantee honesty, and that the assumption that anonymity is necessary is debatable [N2-F2]. Respondent age is another important factor: the classroom-size study shows that classroom size affected peer-reported and self-reported bullying differently, and the evidence suggests that younger students may behave differently in reporting contexts [N4-F3]. In the self-report literature, age likely affects both comprehension and willingness to disclose sensitive experiences, which in turn affects validity [N2-F2].

Overall, self-report methods are strongest when the goal is to capture private or less obvious bullying experiences and when broad, rapid data collection is needed [N2-F2]. Their weaknesses include social desirability bias, recall bias, response style effects, and sensitivity to wording and anonymity choices [N2-F2][N2-R5]. They are also limited by the difficulty of verifying reports and by the fact that younger respondents may interpret bullying differently [N2-F2][N4-F3].

Branch report: practical implementation and contextual tradeoffs

Peer nomination tends to be more feasible or acceptable in school settings when the school environment supports multiple informants and when direct observation is difficult. The peer-report literature describes peer nominations as a common method for measuring aggression because peers can observe classmates in multiple contexts, including less-supervised settings like playgrounds, lunchrooms, and hallways [N1-F1]. This makes peer nomination especially useful in schools where teachers may not be able to observe all bullying incidents directly, and where students are more likely to report incidents that occur in peer settings [N1-F1]. Peer nomination can also be acceptable in settings where students are comfortable identifying others as bullies or victims, although the evidence also notes that peer-report measures can be affected by social desirability and group dynamics [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Self-report methods tend to be more feasible or acceptable in school settings when anonymity and efficiency are priorities. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that self-report surveys are the most frequently used way to evaluate anti-bullying programs and estimate prevalence, and that they are rapid and efficient for large numbers of students [N2-F2]. This makes self-report methods attractive for large-scale school surveys or programs that need quick data collection. The same evidence also notes that self-report measures are usually anonymous, and that anonymity is often assumed to encourage honest reporting [N2-F2]. However, the evidence also questions whether anonymity is always necessary and warns that anonymous surveys can still be difficult to validate because researchers cannot corroborate student reports [N2-F2]. Therefore, self-report methods are more acceptable when students are comfortable disclosing sensitive experiences and when the survey is designed to minimize social pressure, but they may be less acceptable in settings where students feel reluctant to report bullying for fear of consequences [N2-F2].

Implementation choices affect comparability and generalizability. The classroom-size study shows that classroom size was negatively associated with peer-reported bullying and victimization, and that self-reported bullying and victimization were affected differently depending on the sample [N4-F3]. This means that the same bullying measure can yield different results in different classroom contexts, reducing comparability across schools or grades [N4-F3]. The evidence also shows that informant selection matters: peer nominations depend on the composition of the informant group, and peer ratings were uniquely associated with adjustment outcomes in a sample of third, fourth, and fifth graders [N1-F1]. This implies that if researchers want comparable results, they must control for grade level and informant selection [N1-F1]. The same evidence indicates that bullying definition and wording can change prevalence numbers across studies, which further complicates generalizability [N2-R2][N2-R5].

In practical terms, peer nomination is better suited for contexts where multiple informants are available and where bullying is likely to be observed in peer settings, while self-report is better suited for contexts where anonymity, efficiency, and broad coverage are important [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Implementation choices such as wording, anonymity, grade level, classroom size, and informant selection therefore determine whether results are comparable and generalizable across different schools or populations [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F3].

Branch report: how bullying definition and wording affect prevalence estimates

Different bullying definitions can change prevalence numbers across studies because the operationalization of bullying determines which behaviors are counted as bullying. The evidence provided here explicitly notes that prevalence estimates can vary across studies and that bullying definitions matter [N2-R2]. It also states that the choice of the word “bully” in survey items can influence reported bullying behavior [N2-R5]. This indicates that even small changes in how bullying is defined can produce different prevalence estimates. The evidence further supports this by noting that studies using the Olweus Bully/Victim Questionnaire yielded a range of prevalence rates for bullying across countries, and that this range may reflect true differences or uncontrolled factors such as student attitudes toward completing the survey or familiarity with the concept of bullying [N2-F2]. In other words, prevalence estimates are not stable across studies unless definitions are tightly controlled.

Wording such as “bully” or “bullying” affects both self-report and peer-report responses. The evidence states that the word “bully” can influence how students report bullying behavior [N2-R5], and that self-report surveys often use the term “bully” in items [N2-F2]. This wording effect is important because students may interpret the term differently: some may understand “bully” as a one-time aggressive act, while others may associate it with repeated, relational, or power-based harm [N2-R5]. The evidence also notes that the BVQ is the most widely used bullying self-report survey, and that prevalence estimates can vary depending on how bullying is operationalized [N2-R2][N2-F2]. Peer nominations may also be affected by wording because the way students are asked to identify bullies or victims can shape what is reported. Although the evidence here is more explicit about self-report wording, the broader context of peer-report measurement indicates that the phrasing of questions can still influence nominations [N1-F1].

Operational definitions affect comparability and interpretation of prevalence because they determine what counts as bullying. The evidence states that prevalence estimates vary across studies, and that the behavior-based scales used in some studies offer a self-report bullying measurement that includes power imbalance, concrete actions, and other features [N6-R3]. This means that a measure that emphasizes power imbalance may report higher bullying prevalence than a measure that focuses only on physical or verbal aggression. The evidence also emphasizes that effective prevention efforts depend on accurate, reliable measures that resonate with youth [N6-R5]. In practice, this means that prevalence estimates cannot be directly compared across studies if the operational definitions differ; researchers must therefore specify the definition used and interpret prevalence accordingly [N2-R2][N6-R3]. The evidence also supports the broader conclusion that bullying definitions matter because they affect both how bullying is measured and how prevalence is interpreted [N2-R2][N2-R5].
